source: seed (original case written for this app)
title: Assam tea estate company: what next?
opening: Our client owns 12 tea estates in Assam and sells most of its tea through auctions. It has been loss-making for three years. The board is asking: should we sell some estates, invest to turn them around, or move into branded tea? What would you advise?
client_context: Produces ~18 million kg of made tea a year, mostly CTC. Estates are a mix of old bushes and newer plantings. Labour is ~60% of production cost and wages are set by state regulation.
objective: Recommend a strategic direction that returns the company to profitability within three years.

clarifications.answer: Revenue ~₹400 cr, operating loss ~₹30 cr last year. The company has limited cash and moderate debt.
Auction prices for CTC tea have been flat in nominal terms for five years while wages have risen ~8% a year.
The board is open to any combination, including selling estates.

data.label: Estate-level economics
data.content: Cost of production ranges from ₹190/kg at the best estates to ₹310/kg at the worst. Average auction realisation is ₹220/kg for most estates; three estates with better quality realise ₹280/kg.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about estate-level profitability or cost variation.

data.label: Branded tea
data.content: Branded packaged tea earns ₹350-450/kg equivalent net of distribution but needs heavy marketing; national brands dominate. Regional brands succeed mostly in their home states. Building a brand would take ~₹60-80 cr over 3 years.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about branded tea or moving downstream.

data.label: Estate sale market
data.content: Buyers exist for estates with good bushes and yields. Low-yield estates sell for little more than land value; some have been sold to smallholder-aggregator companies.
data.release_when: Candidate asks about selling estates or what they're worth.

exhibits.title: Estate portfolio: yield and cost of production
exhibits.release_when: Candidate asks to segment the estates or compare their performance.
takeaways: Group A is highly profitable (+₹90/kg), B is roughly break-even (-₹5/kg), and C is deeply loss-making (-₹95/kg).
The company's losses come mostly from group C.

quant.question: Where do the losses come from?
quant.solution: Output 18 mn kg. A: 5.4 mn kg × +₹90 = +₹49 cr. B: 8.1 mn kg × -₹5 = -₹4 cr. C: 4.5 mn kg × -₹95 = -₹43 cr. Net ≈ +₹2 cr at estate level; with ~₹32 cr of corporate overheads, operating loss ≈ ₹30 cr. So C destroys ~₹43 cr.
quant.answer: Group C loses ~₹43 cr; A earns ~₹49 cr

analytical_paths: Segment the portfolio before choosing an option: which estates make and lose money, and why → fix/sell/invest decisions differ by estate group → branded tea tested as an option for A's quality tea.
Option-evaluation approach: define criteria (profit impact, investment, risk, time), then evaluate the three board options, informed by portfolio data.
key_insights: It isn't one company-wide answer: estate group C (old bushes, low yield) causes almost all the loss, and A is very profitable.
Sell or restructure C (e.g. lease to smallholder aggregators, or replant over time), fix B's cost, and protect A.
Branded tea is a costly, slow bet that competes with national brands; a premium/direct channel for group A's quality tea is a more realistic step.
reference_solution: Reframe the board's either/or: segment the estates. The exhibit shows A profitable, B break-even and C losing ~₹43 cr. Sell or restructure C (land value plus smallholder partnerships), run a cost and yield programme in B (mechanised plucking, infilling), and move A's high-quality output from auctions to private sales, exports and a small premium/online brand rather than a full national brand. That returns the company to profit within ~2 years.
alternative_approaches: An option-evaluation matrix (sell / turnaround / brand) that ends with a mixed answer by estate.
A 'replant C' option with a long payback (tea bushes take ~4-5 years to mature) can be defended if the candidate quantifies the cash need.
recommendation: Don't pick one option for the whole company. (1) Exit or restructure the 4 group-C estates (sale, or lease to smallholder aggregators): removes ~₹43 cr of losses. (2) Run a 2-year productivity programme in the 5 group-B estates. (3) Take group A's premium tea direct: private sales, exports and a small premium online brand, instead of betting ₹60-80 cr on a national brand. Result: profitable within ~2 years. Risks: labour relations and government approvals for estate sales, and auction price volatility.
interviewer_notes: The board's framing is a trap: good candidates segment before choosing.
Unfamiliar industry: reward first-principles reasoning about yield, cost and realisation.
common_pitfalls: Picking one of the three options for the whole company.
Jumping to branding because margins look higher.
learning_objective: Segment a portfolio before answering a strategic either/or question.
